name: Potassium
summary: Potassium is a mineral that lets nerves send signals and muscles, including the heart, contract normally. It also works against the effect of salt (sodium) on blood pressure. The kidneys keep the blood level in a narrow range, so both too little and too much in the blood can be dangerous.
roles: Fluid balance inside and outside cells
Balancing the effect of sodium on blood pressure

status.note: A blood potassium test shows whether the level in the blood is safe, not how much potassium a person eats: healthy kidneys keep the blood level in range across a wide range of intakes. A low or high result usually comes from medicines, vomiting or diarrhoea, or kidney function rather than diet, and a falsely high result is common when the blood sample is damaged. Research estimates intake from potassium in 24-hour urine. eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate) and creatinine show how well the kidneys work, which decides whether extra potassium is safe.

signs: Paralysis or dangerous heart rhythms, when very low
atRisk: People taking loop or thiazide water pills (diuretics)
Long-lasting vomiting or diarrhoea, or overuse of laxatives
Diets low in fruit and vegetables (low intake is linked to higher blood pressure, but rarely lowers blood potassium on its own)

signs: Often no symptoms until it is dangerous
Slow or irregular heartbeat, which can stop the heart
high.note: High blood potassium (hyperkalaemia) is a medical emergency because it can disturb the heart rhythm. It mostly happens when the kidneys cannot remove potassium: in kidney disease, and with some blood pressure and heart medicines (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and potassium-sparing water pills such as spironolactone). EFSA notes that in people with reduced kidney function, harm to the heart has been reported with as little as 1 g of extra potassium a day from supplements or low-sodium salts, on top of food. In healthy adults, single very large amounts (5–7 g) from supplements have caused heart problems in case reports. Potassium from ordinary food is considered low risk for healthy people.

examples: Fruit such as bananas, oranges and dried apricots
Vegetables such as spinach, tomatoes and mushrooms
foodSources.note: With kidney disease, a doctor or dietitian may advise limiting high-potassium foods, and this app then hides potassium-rich food suggestions.

forms.name: Potassium chloride
forms.note: The usual form for treating low blood potassium, often on prescription, as tablets, fizzy tablets or liquid. EFSA notes that some slow-release tablets have irritated or damaged the gut lining; the risk depended more on the tablet type than on the amount.

forms.name: Potassium citrate and potassium bicarbonate
forms.note: Alkaline forms. Potassium citrate is used under medical care to prevent some kidney stones. Both have been studied for bone health.

forms.name: Potassium gluconate and other supplement salts
forms.note: Found in over-the-counter supplements and multivitamins. The amount of potassium per tablet varies a lot between products and countries.

forms.name: Salt substitutes (low-sodium salt)
forms.note: Part of the sodium chloride is replaced with potassium chloride (for example 25 % in the large SSaSS trial). They are an easily overlooked potassium source, which matters with kidney disease or medicines that raise potassium.

forms.name: Potassium iodide
forms.note: A source of iodine, not of potassium: it is used in iodised salt and, in radiation emergencies, as tablets that protect the thyroid when authorities advise it. See iodine.

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA (2005) found the data insufficient to set an upper limit for potassium, and none has been set since. Potassium from food (up to 5–6 g a day in adults) is considered low risk for generally healthy people, and about 3 g a day of extra potassium chloride for a long time caused no harm in healthy adults in studies. But supplements can cause stomach and gut problems, single very large amounts have harmed the heart, and people with reduced kidney function, diabetes, heart medicines that affect potassium, dehydration from hard exercise, or older age are more sensitive. In people with reduced kidney function, harm has been reported with about 1 g a day extra from supplements or low-sodium salts. No upper limit does not mean that any amount from supplements is safe.

sources.title: Opinion of the Scientific Panel on Dietetic products, nutrition and allergies [NDA] on a request from the Commission related to the Tolerable Upper Intake Level of Potassium
Dietary Reference Values for nutrients Summary report

interactions.note: Weak kidneys can't remove extra potassium, so supplements, potassium salt substitutes and sometimes potassium-rich foods can raise blood potassium to dangerous levels. Talk to your doctor before any change.

interactions.with: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (e.g. ramipril, lisinopril, losartan, valsartan)
interactions.note: These blood pressure and heart medicines make the kidneys keep potassium. Adding potassium supplements or salt substitutes can push blood potassium too high. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

interactions.with: Potassium-sparing water pills (e.g. spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene)
interactions.note: They raise blood potassium on purpose. Extra potassium from supplements or salt substitutes can be dangerous with them.

interactions.with: Other water pills (loop and thiazide diuretics, e.g. furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide)
interactions.note: They make the body lose potassium, which is why doctors sometimes check potassium and may prescribe it. Not something to correct without a blood test.
EFSA lists people with diabetes among the groups more sensitive to high blood potassium.

cautions: With kidney disease, or with medicines that raise potassium, talk to your doctor before using potassium supplements or salt substitutes.
Salt substitutes (low-sodium salt) contain potassium, even though the label says salt.
Blood potassium outside the normal range needs a doctor, not a supplement or a diet change on your own.
EFSA set no upper limit for potassium, but that does not mean large supplement amounts are safe.

commonUses: May help lower blood pressure, especially in people whose blood pressure is high.
May ease or prevent muscle cramps.
May support heart and stroke health.
May support bone health by reducing calcium lost in urine.

origin: Potassium is a mineral and an electrolyte, a substance that carries an electric charge in body fluids. It helps nerves send signals and muscles, including the heart, contract. The body cannot make it, so it comes from food such as potatoes, beans, fruit and vegetables.

Potassium supplements are made by purifying potassium salts from mineral deposits or by chemical production. The usual forms are potassium chloride, potassium citrate, potassium bicarbonate and potassium gluconate. Salt substitutes also contain potassium chloride.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets an adequate intake (AI) of 3,500 mg a day for adults and in pregnancy, and 4,000 mg when breastfeeding. EFSA found too little data to set a tolerable upper intake level (the most that is likely safe every day), and none has been set since. That does not mean any supplement amount is safe: stomach and gut problems, and harm to the heart from single very large amounts, have been reported. These are population values, not personal targets.
Amounts used in studies of potassium supplements vary a lot, and there is no single common amount. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When checking a label, look at which form it is (potassium chloride, citrate, bicarbonate or gluconate) and how much potassium, not compound weight, is in one serving, because the two numbers differ. Slow-release tablets have irritated the gut lining in some cases. Salt substitutes (low-sodium salt) are an easily missed source. People with kidney disease, diabetes, or who take ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers or potassium-sparing water pills should talk to their doctor before using potassium supplements or salt substitutes, because blood potassium can rise to dangerous levels.

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes. The adequate intake can be reached from ordinary food, mainly from potatoes, pulses, fruit, vegetables, fish and dairy, if the diet has plenty of these. A supplement is not needed to get there for most people. The larger amount used in studies is difficult to reach from food alone and is not meant as a goal. For example, for the EFSA adequate intake, adults, about 190 g of dried apricots, or about 580 g of baked potato with skin.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the food named. Cooked, stored or processed foods and other brands differ. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed.
